cards.#1: Show Out took a Ping s159 apart, laser-cut the head and put it back together as a single numbered piece. Tropical Noir exists once and sold once, which is what 1/1 means. At $500 it is the more expensive of the two Artist Series wedges.
cards.#2: THE WATCHER is the other Artist Series piece, engraved on a Titleist Vokey 56 and sold at $450. Vincent Newman works out of a unit in Gilbert, Arizona, and the shipping address on his own site is a house. That is the scale this whole tier operates at.
cards.#3: Stencil Lab is the pre-set tier, a fixed design applied to the wedge you send in, and it costs less than a commission because nobody is drawing it from scratch. Show Out photograph these on engraving plates rather than on a club, so the plate is what you are looking at. Their line for the shop: serious about quality, casual about rules.
cards.#4: Show Out sell Butch T. Cougar as a pre-set at $150, a college mascot rendered in engraving. The photograph is their sample plate rather than a finished club, because the design goes on whatever wedge you send them. That is the trade in this tier, where you know the drawing before you ship the club.
cards.#5: Desert Diamondback is the cheapest way into Show Out at $135, and it is Arizona iconography from a shop that sits in Arizona. It is pictured as an engraving sample rather than a finished club, which is how the whole Stencil Lab range gets shown.
cards.#6: Desert Drought Golf is Phoenix humour at $135, in a state where the water conversation is not much of a joke. Show Out photograph it on a sample plate like the rest of the pre-set designs, so the club that ends up in your bag is the one you already own.
cards.#7: The commission route starts at $125 for entry-level engraving, runs to $250 for Signature and $375 for Complex, and ends with a club that exists once. You send your own wedge and agree a design, and the head comes off the shaft before anything else happens, so the shaft never sees heat. The head is then annealed, sanded, buffed and sealed with wax.
cards.#8: Bettinardi built one left-handed three-wedge set in Texas Tea and put it in the Hive, which is the closest thing a major maker does to a one-off. Fifty-two, fifty-six and sixty degrees, $1000 for all three, and no second set behind it when this one goes.
cards.#9: Zombee Black PVD is another single left-handed set, 50, 54 and 58 degrees at $1200. The names are not focus-grouped, which is most of the appeal of the Hive — Bettinardi treats these drops as objects rather than as inventory to be replenished. Black PVD on a left-handed set narrows the audience to almost nobody.
cards.#10: Steel Patina is the finish that changes colour with use rather than holding its look, which makes it the odd one out among collector pieces. Bettinardi built one left-handed set at $1100, 52, 56 and 60 degrees. It will not look like the photograph a year from now.
cards.#11: Indi puts the groove choice at checkout — conforming, or the non-conforming set they label Big Box Grooves and mark Not Tournament Approved. The nickel chrome Blast Face 4 is $170 with either. Choosing at the cart is the part that makes it custom, and the part that decides what you can enter it in.
cards.#12: The bronze version of the same head is also $170, and bronze is the finish people choose when they want a wedge to look used quickly. Indi work out of Carlsbad, California, in a fitting studio they call the House of Spin, which tells you how seriously they take the sales floor.
cards.#13: FLX is the straighter leading edge, built for pickers and firm turf, and ATK is the other grind Indi offer. Same $170, same Blast Face head, and the decision is about how much ground you take rather than about how the club looks behind the ball.
cards.#14: Indi sell the B.I.G. Bunker Beater as a dedicated sand club at $129, well under half of what most wedges around it cost. A club built for one shot is an unfashionable idea, and at that price it does not have to earn a permanent slot in the bag.
cards.#15: New Level forge the SPN V3 in raw 1020 carbon, which will rust, and sell it at $149 with a build configurator that runs to length in quarter-inch steps and about seventy shafts. They ship internationally and say so plainly, which is not the standard among makers at this end of the market.
cards.#16: Desert Eclipse is the previous SPN generation, on closeout at $100. New Level do not take returns on anything, because everything is built after you order it, and a closeout price does not change the policy. Order the loft and the length you actually play.
cards.#17: Edel charge one price across every loft, grind, bounce and weight-bias combination, so the SMS Pro is $180 whatever you build. The flip weight shifts mass to the heel or the toe depending on how you order it, which means two of these can sit differently behind the ball at the same spec.
cards.#18: The Stick’em is PXG’s configurable wedge, built to what you enter rather than pulled off a rack. Chrome is the $199 version and the cheaper of the two finishes. It is the most conventional-looking club in the range and the one that will date the slowest.
cards.#19: The black Stick’em is the same configurable wedge at $219, which is twenty dollars for the finish and nothing else. Black sits quieter behind the ball for anyone who finds chrome glare distracting at address, and it will wear through at the leading edge in the same time.
cards.#20: The BARRETT is the Patrick Reed signature wedge, priced in yen at ¥37,950 and sold at home in Japan. Outside Japan you go through a distributor, which is the arrangement for everything Grindworks make. It is the most expensive of their three wedges by a wide margin.
cards.#21: The 86 RAW is SUS218 stainless, vibratory tumbled to a marbled raw finish, and it comes in four factory grinds at ¥27,500. Patrick Reed is credited with the spec. The finish is the reason to look at it, since a tumbled head reads mottled rather than uniform and keeps moving as the steel goes.
cards.#22: The ZIP is the cheapest thing Grindworks make at ¥20,020, and it is still built to order after you buy it. That is the Grindworks position in one club. Nothing sits on a shelf waiting, whatever it costs, and the wait is the same at the bottom of the range as at the top.
cards.#23: Fourteen sell the FRZ head two ways. Stock is $250 and ships as built; Forged Custom is made to order in about twenty business days and is non-returnable even unused. That second condition is stated plainly on their own pages, which is more than most makers manage.
cards.#24: Fourteen was founded in 1981 by Takamitsu Takebayashi, an accomplished amateur who started out designing clubs for other people’s brands. The DJ-6 is the $220 stock wedge in that line, and a company built by a designer-for-hire tends to know what a shape is supposed to do.
cards.#25: KYOEI CUSTOM lets you choose the back design, the sole grind and the stamping, which is a deeper menu than most configurators put in front of you. The price carries no currency label anywhere on their site, so the 265.00 to 359.00 range appears exactly as they publish it.
cards.#26: KYOEI describe the Tour wedge on their own page as one hundred per cent made and hand-ground in Japan, and their Heritage page roots the company in Himeji. The range runs 265.00 to 349.00, again with no currency attached to the number, and they ship worldwide.
cards.#27: Three machined ports take interchangeable weights, which is how the Triple Weight moves its balance without changing the shape of the head. KYOEI also sell a non-conforming version of this one, openly, which very few makers will do under their own name. The range runs 280.00 to 374.00.
cards.#28: The Y Grind is named after Yoshitaka Miura, which tells you where it sits in the line. QPQ is the hardest of the three finishes Miura offer, and at $385 this is the most expensive way to buy the shape. Hard finishes hold their look longer on a club that lives in sand.
cards.#29: Miura’s configurator goes deeper than anyone else’s: lie and loft in two-degree ranges either way, length in quarter inches, thirteen shaft brands, and a free-text box for swing-weight targets. The K-Grind 2.0 at $300 is the cheapest head you can run through it, and the configurator is where the money goes.
cards.#30: Raw is the finish that patinas, so the $320 Y Grind will look different by the end of a season and different again the year after. The head is forged in Himeji, though the company you actually buy from is Miura Golf LLC in Scottsdale.
cards.#31: Every Artisan wedge is hand-ground by Mike Taylor, formerly Nike’s tour grinder, who signs the copy on their own site “- MT”. Stamping and paint fill are included in the $350 starting price rather than charged on top. Right hand only, which rules out a good number of people before they start.
cards.#32: The finishes run heat-torched Bluebonnet, Texas Crude PVD, Oxidado and Patina Grey, and the upcharge is thirty to sixty dollars on top of the wedge. The queue after your fitting runs nine weeks, which is the part people tend to forget about when they are booking the flight to Texas.

kickers.1: Show Out works one club at a time, on a wedge you already own. You ship it, the head comes off the shaft, the design goes on, and it comes back numbered 1/1 because there is exactly one of each.
kickers.2: Everything here is made after you order it, which is not the same thing as bespoke. You choose from a menu — grind, finish, loft, lie, length, shaft, ferrule — and you cannot ask for what is not on it.
kickers.3: Four Japanese makers have four different answers to whether you can actually buy one. Grindworks sells at home in yen and sends everyone else to a distributor. Miura is forged in Himeji, though the storefront you buy from is a US company in Scottsdale.
kickers.4: Artisan will hand-grind a wedge and stamp it however you like, but only after you fly to Texas and sit a half-day fitting. That is not a marketing posture; it is written plainly on their own site.
kickers.5: Every major maker runs a wedge personalisation program. Two of them publish what the limits actually are, and the rest hide the options behind a configurator that renders nothing until you are already inside it.
